stem: Which section of the Constitution of Zimbabwe sets out the rights of children?

options.content: section 81
options.rationale: Correct: section 81 deals with the rights of children.

options.content: section 80
options.rationale: Section 80 deals with the rights of women.

options.content: section 83
options.rationale: Section 83 deals with persons with disabilities.

options.content: section 162
options.rationale: Section 162 lists the courts.

explanation: Section 81, in the Declaration of Rights (Chapter 4), sets out children's rights.

stem: Under the Constitution of Zimbabwe, a child is any person under the age of …

options.content: 18 years
options.rationale: Correct: every boy and girl under 18 is a child.

options.content: 16 years
options.rationale: 16 is not the constitutional age; childhood ends at 18.

options.content: 21 years
options.rationale: 21 was once the age of majority in some laws; today it is 18.

options.content: 13 years
options.rationale: A 13-year-old is still a child; childhood ends at 18.

explanation: Section 81 defines a child as every boy and girl under the age of 18.

stem: Which of the following is a **responsibility** of a child at school, not a right?

options.content: receiving an education
options.rationale: This is a right.

options.content: being safe from bullying and abuse
options.rationale: This is a right.

options.content: being heard on matters that affect them
options.rationale: This is a right.

options.content: obeying school rules
options.rationale: Correct: this is something the child must do.

explanation: A responsibility is a duty the child carries out. Education, safety and being heard are rights others must respect.

stem: Which international agreement, adopted in 1989, is the main treaty on children's rights?

options.content: the African Charter on the Rights and Welfare of the Child
options.rationale: This African treaty was adopted in 1990.

options.content: the Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination against Women
options.rationale: CEDAW (1979) deals with women's rights.

options.content: the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child
options.rationale: Correct: adopted by the UN General Assembly in 1989.

options.content: the SADC Protocol on Gender and Development
options.rationale: This 2008 protocol deals with gender.

explanation: The UN Convention on the Rights of the Child (1989) is the main international treaty; the African Charter (1990) applies across Africa.

stem: Tafadzwa, aged 13, is kept at home every school day to herd cattle and has not attended school this year. Which right is **most clearly** denied?

options.content: the right to vote in elections
options.rationale: Voting begins at 18; it is not a child's right.

options.content: the right to education
options.rationale: Correct: he is kept from school.

options.content: the right to own land in his own name
options.rationale: This is not the issue in the scenario.

options.content: the right to choose his own religion
options.rationale: Nothing in the scenario concerns religion.

explanation: Missing school to work every day denies the right to education and may also be child labour, from which section 81 protects children.

stem: A school sets up a suggestion box and a pupils' council. Which right does this **mainly** uphold?

options.content: the right to health care
options.rationale: A suggestion box does not provide health care.

options.content: the right to be heard
options.rationale: Correct: pupils can raise their views.

options.content: the right to shelter
options.rationale: Shelter is a right at home; this is not about shelter.

options.content: the right to a name and birth certificate
options.rationale: This right is upheld by birth registration, not a suggestion box.

explanation: Suggestion boxes and councils let pupils express views on matters that affect them: the right to be heard.
hints: What can pupils do with a suggestion box?

stem: What does the principle of the **best interests of the child** mean?

options.content: Children may do whatever they want without guidance
options.rationale: Children still need guidance; the principle is about decisions made for them.

options.content: Parents' wishes must always come before the welfare of the child
options.rationale: The child's welfare comes first.

options.content: The child with the best results receives the most help
options.rationale: The principle applies to every child, not to the best performers.

options.content: In matters concerning a child, what is best for the child comes first
options.rationale: Correct: section 81 says the child's best interests are paramount.

explanation: Section 81 says a child's best interests are paramount in every matter concerning the child.

stem: Why are children's rights given special protection in the Constitution?

options.content: Children pay more taxes than adults
options.rationale: Children generally do not pay income tax.

options.content: Children are able to vote in all elections
options.rationale: Voting begins at 18.

options.content: Children elect their own members to make the laws of the country in Parliament
options.rationale: Parliament is made up of adults.

options.content: Children depend on adults and cannot always protect themselves
options.rationale: Correct: children are vulnerable.

explanation: Children rely on adults for their needs and safety, so the law gives them special protection.
hints: Think about why children are a vulnerable group.

stem: The African Charter on the Rights and Welfare of the Child also lists the responsibilities of children.
explanation: True. Unusually, the African Charter (1990) sets out children's responsibilities as well as their rights.

stem: A child who misbehaves loses the right to education.
explanation: False. Rights belong to every child. A school may discipline a pupil, but the right to education is not taken away as a punishment.

stem: Match each right with a matching responsibility.

left.content: the right to a safe environment
the right to shelter and care

right.content: helping with household chores suitable for one's age
working hard and letting others learn

explanation: Many rights carry a matching responsibility that helps others enjoy the same right.

payload.template: Children's rights are set out in section {{blank:a}} of the Constitution. The African Charter on the Rights and Welfare of the Child was adopted in {{blank:b}}.

explanation: Section 81; the African Charter in 1990. The UN Convention on the Rights of the Child was adopted in 1989.

payload.template: Education is a {{blank:a}} of every child. Doing homework is a {{blank:b}} of a pupil.

explanation: Education is an entitlement (a right); homework is a duty (a responsibility).
hints: Is it something you receive or something you do?

stem: Name the government department to which a case of a neglected child can be reported, besides the police.
explanation: The **Department of Social Welfare** (social services) protects neglected and abused children. The Registrar General registers births.

stem: State **two** rights and **two** responsibilities of a child at home.

points.description: Right: any one of: shelter, food, clothing, care and love, security/protection from abuse, a name/birth certificate, health care, education, play and rest
Right: a second different right
Responsibility: any one of: respecting parents and elders, helping with age-appropriate chores, looking after younger siblings, caring for family property, keeping oneself safe
Responsibility: a second different responsibility

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Rights: shelter and protection from abuse. Responsibilities: respecting parents and elders, and helping with household chores.

explanation: One mark per correct right and responsibility; they must be correctly labelled.

stem: Explain **two** reasons why it is important for children to carry out their responsibilities at school.

points.description: Identifies learning / discipline
Explains that obeying rules and working hard lets the child and others learn, so results improve
Identifies respect and safety / preparing for citizenship
Explains that respecting others and caring for property keeps the school safe and prepares children to be responsible citizens

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: When pupils obey rules and work hard, lessons run smoothly and everyone can learn, so the child and classmates achieve better results. Respecting others and caring for school property keeps the school safe and pleasant, and it prepares children to be responsible citizens.

explanation: One mark for each reason and one for its explanation.
hints: Think of learning and of the kind of adult the child becomes.

stem: Nyasha, aged 11, tells her teacher that an older relative beats her often and that she sometimes goes without food. Suggest **two** things the teacher should do, and explain why.

points.description: Suggests reporting to the head teacher and the Department of Social Welfare or the police Victim Friendly Unit
Explains that the child's right to protection from abuse and neglect (section 81) must be upheld by the authorities
Suggests listening calmly, keeping her safe and providing immediate support (e.g. food from a school feeding scheme, referral to a clinic)
Explains that the child's best interests come first and she must feel safe to speak

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: The teacher should report the case to the head teacher and to the Department of Social Welfare or the police Victim Friendly Unit, because Nyasha's right to protection from abuse and neglect must be upheld by people with the power to act. The teacher should also listen calmly, make sure she is safe at school and arrange immediate help such as food or a clinic visit, because her best interests come first.

explanation: Credit sensible actions (1 each) with explanations linked to her rights or welfare (1 each).
hints: Who has the power to protect her, and what does she need today?

stem:
**Source A** — a report in a fictional school newsletter, Bindura, 2026 (invented for this question)

> This term our school council asked for a safer path to school after two pupils were nearly hit by cars. The head teacher took the request to the school development committee, which asked the council for a pedestrian crossing. Meanwhile, Form 2 pupils agreed to walk in groups and to report any bullying on the path. The crossing will be built next month.

Read Source A and answer the questions.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Which right did the pupils use when the school council made its request?

options.content: the right to vote
options.rationale: Pupils are under 18; the council request was not an election.

options.content: the right to a name
options.rationale: The request was not about names.

options.content: the right to be heard
options.rationale: Correct: they raised their concern through the council.

options.content: the right to shelter
options.rationale: The request was about safety on the path, not shelter.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Identify **two** responsibilities the Form 2 pupils accepted.

points.description: Walking in groups (keeping themselves safe)
Reporting bullying on the path

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Walking to school in groups and reporting any bullying on the path.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Explain how the source shows rights and responsibilities working together.

points.description: The pupils used their right to be heard to raise a safety problem
Adults (head, committee, council) upheld the right to safety by acting on it
The pupils carried out responsibilities (walking in groups, reporting bullying) that protect themselves and others

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: The pupils used their right to be heard to raise the problem. The head teacher, committee and council upheld the right to a safe environment by arranging a crossing. Meanwhile the pupils carried out responsibilities, walking in groups and reporting bullying, which protected themselves and others.

explanation: A source-based practice item on the right to be heard and matching responsibilities.
hints: In (c), show what the pupils claimed, what adults did and what the pupils did.

stem: This question is about children's rights in Zimbabwe.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Describe **two** ways in which children's rights are protected in Zimbabwe.

points.description: The Constitution (section 81) sets out rights, and courts can enforce them; international treaties (UN Convention, African Charter)
Institutions: the Department of Social Welfare, the police Victim Friendly Unit, schools, assistance such as BEAM

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Section 81 of the Constitution sets out children's rights, and the courts can enforce them; Zimbabwe also follows international treaties such as the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child. Institutions such as the Department of Social Welfare and the police Victim Friendly Unit act when children are abused or neglected, and programmes such as BEAM help poor children pay school fees.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: "Children in Zimbabwe enjoy all their rights." How far do you agree?

points.description: For: strong legal protection in section 81; most children attend school; birth registration, clinics and school feeding where available
Against: some children miss school because of fees or poverty; child labour; abuse and neglect; lack of birth certificates in some areas
Against: awareness and enforcement are uneven, especially in remote areas
Supported judgement

levels.descriptor: Developed explanation of several relevant points or arguments, supported by accurate, specific knowledge and examples, considering more than one side and reaching a supported judgement that answers the question.
Developed explanation of some factors or arguments with relevant supporting detail; a judgement is attempted but is only partly supported, or the other side is thin.
Some explanation of one or two relevant factors, or several points described with limited explanation; little or no judgement.
Simple, general or narrative statements with limited relevance to the question; little explanation.

answerSpec.modelAnswer:
There is evidence for the statement. Section 81 of the Constitution gives children a full set of rights, and the courts, the Department of Social Welfare and the police can enforce them. Most children attend school, and programmes such as BEAM help poor families with fees.

However, many children do not enjoy all their rights. Some miss school because their families cannot afford fees or need them to work, which may be child labour. Some children suffer abuse or neglect, and some in remote areas lack birth certificates, which makes it hard to enrol in school later. Awareness of rights and enforcement are uneven.

I disagree with the statement. The law protects children well on paper, but poverty, harmful practices and weak enforcement mean that not all children enjoy all their rights in practice.

explanation: A practice evaluative item on how far children enjoy their rights.
hints: In (b), separate what the law says from what happens in practice.
